title: Childhood in Donaldsonville: first school and father's hotel work
summary: He recalls his first school, the family's Donaldsonville home, the move around 1915, and his father's hard jobs and night-desk work at the hotel, plus playing now and then with a second local band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Uh-huh. And I remember the street that we lived on was the head of running, go to railroad street, which is about half a block. There was a store named Babin, B-A-U-B-I-N, we used to trade from. And, uh, I went to a public school going towards railroad street, going towards, from my house, to the railroad station. But, uh, my first school was through a, a colored lady named Miss, uh, Rita. Mm-hmm. So I was a little private, a primary school, you know, where you go and learn your APCs and everything. And from there I went to this public school. They had a, a Catholic school there for, for the colored term, but, I mean, my people didn't send me there. They sent me to this school. And eventually we left, uh, we moved out of Donaldsonville around, I'd say about 1915. Uh-huh. And, uh, my father, the reason for the family was in, uh, Donaldsonville because that was my mother's home, and she had a home there with my grandfather. And the thing was kind of tough, and my dad, my dad would go in the city and find work, see, because he couldn't find work around Donaldsonville so much, see. And finally I remember he did come to Donaldsonville and they got him a job at, uh, the hotel. I think it was Hotel Donaldsonville, one of the biggest hotels they had there. And I remember, well, my dad used to sometime play a game. They had another band. Uh, uh, it was from out, uh, had a place called Frogamore. That was on the other side of the railroad track in Donaldsonville. Well, uh, Clayborne was a D-Light band, you see. And my daddy could play with them, but they was already, they already had the number of men that they needed, you see. But they knew all of them, and sometimes he'd go play with the Sunderband, and they used to kid him by playing with the Trashy Band. But that was, you know, they had to make a little money, you see. And then one time I remember he worked on, um, like a hauling, uh, in the railroad station, uh, fooling with trunks and things. Because I remember my mother used to have to rub his back when he'd come home and he had to quit that job, because it was too hard for him. But he finally got a job in, uh, in the hotel where he was sort of, uh, pulled in a night desk man, you know. Oh, I see. He used to come around and tell us kids where he tells about his particular night's work, you know, and everything. And that's how he'd become the new, a lot of the nice and rich white people around Donaldsonville, you see.
